column4: Construction of a Food Safety and Quality Assurance in Support for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
column6:
Component 1: Construction of Food Processing and Labeling/Packaging Center for Food Standardization - P20,000,000.00
Establishment of a center that would process, mass produce and package food products developed from VSU research and development activities as well as assist entrepreneurs in food processing, labeling and packaging. Establishment of a laboratory accredited by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to analyze and certify the contents and nutritional analysis of food products.

Component 2: Construction of the Food Quality Assurance  Center and Purchase of Equipment and Fixtures -P60,000,000.00 (P40,000,000.00 Infrastructure for 2020, P20,000,000.00 Purchase of Equipment for 2021 and 2022)
Quality has become an important issue in agri-business and food industry. Assurance and sustainability of food quality and safety should be the primary concern of every manufacturer and consumers.  The Food Quality Assurance Center will provide the following services to clientele: laboratory services (physical, microbiological and chemical analyses), food standardization, product designing and development of new products, product quality improvement, assessment and evaluation of raw material and product safety, and determination and establishment of shelf life. This facility should have adequate laboratory facilities equipped with more sophisticated instruments, apparatus and library facilities as required.

The government thrust towards boosting productivity and enhancing competitiveness among food enterprises belonging to the MSMEs in the different regions is currently felt in Visayas State University (VSU) with the sustained support towards the establishment of a food testing laboratory programmed to cater the needs of Region 8. This said facility will be able to assess the nutritional quality of foods necessary for the compliance of packaging and labeling of foods intended for local and international markets and the eventual licensing of the concerned enterprises. The second phase of this Food Testing Laboratory costing 20M pesos will be launched early next year (2019). The renovation cost of the building for the facility located at the Department of Food Science and Technology is sourced from the university’s STF (income from tuition) amounting to 3.3M pesos.
However, even with the abovementioned facility, the MSMEs will still be handicapped with other issues relating to quality vis-à-vis established standards which are more and more strictly implemented with the growing consciousness for safety and wellness issues. Hence, the need for a Food Quality Assurance program/center to provide a professional seal of approval for a food product to be released to the market with guaranteed safety and shelf life. Such a seal can only be done using appropriate and adequate methods and equipment. Moreover, the construction of a separate facility for food quality assurance will support the BS Food Technology and MS Food Science and Technology programs and the upcoming offering of PhD Food Science of the department including the department’s research and extension activities and the university in general. The realization of this proposed project will become an additional avenue for the development and production of globally competent graduates in science and technology with cutting-edge scientific knowledge for sustainable communities and environment.

column6: The Agriculture and Fisheries Regulatory Support Program (AFRSP) plays a vital role in safeguarding food safety, market access, and agricultural productivity in the Philippines. Integrated with the PREXC system, AFRSP manages regulatory affairs from national to local levels, ensuring compliance with food safety standards through inspections and rigorous quality control, protecting public health and boosting consumer confidence. column4: Completion of Fish Processing and Aquaculture Laboratory
column6:
The establishment of the Aquaculture and Fish Processing Laboratory at the College of Fisheries, Mindanao State University – General Santos, is a strategic initiative aimed at enhancing education, research, and community extension in the fields of aquaculture, fisheries, and fish processing. The laboratory will serve as a modern, fully equipped venue where students can gain hands-on experience in aquaculture and fish processing activities, directly applying the knowledge acquired from their courses. It will also support the hosting of scientific activities, workshops, and conferences in the fields of biology and fisheries, allowing the College to showcase recent laboratory research, innovations, and extension programs.

The facility is designed to be highly sustainable and impactful, benefiting both students—who are future aquaculturists and fish processors—and local communities, contributing to food security and livelihood development in the region. The laboratory will complement the College’s existing research station, which has been operational for over 20 years and now requires rehabilitation. The new structure will house specialized laboratory areas, including:

Aquaculture Laboratories: Phycology, Ichthyology, Feed and Nutrition, and Fish Health and Diseases.

Fish Processing Laboratories: Sensory and Evaluation Analysis, Chemistry, and Microbiology.

column4: Construction of Food Innovation Center (FIC)

The participation of both men and women in various beneficiary groups in problem identification and project design was crucial in the planning process of the project. In addition, it covers the installation of basic electrical and plumbing systems, water supply and drainage lines, and provisions for future connections to upper floors. The first phase of construction aims to ensure that the ground floor becomes fully functional and ready for use by the university. The finished ground floor will house

Thus, completing this phase will allow BukSU to begin initial operations and utilization of the facility, while subsequent phases focus on constructing the upper floors and installing specialized equipment and fixtures. To realize these objectives, the completed ground floor will be designed with key

column4: Integrated  Nutrition and Food Security Project
column6:
Childhood undernutrition was estimated to have cost the Philippine economy US$4.4 billion. The country ranks sixth among East Asian and Pacific countries with the highest prevalence of stunting and is among the top ten countries in the world with the highest number of stunted children. In 2019, one in three children (29%) under the age of five suffered from stunting, or being undersized for their age (World Bank 2021).

The project will target NCR and the regions with highest levels of stunting- Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao 45% of children below five are stunted, in Southwestern Tagalog Region (MIMAROPA) 41%, Bicol Region it is 40%, Western Visayas 40%, and in the south-central Mindanao Region (SOCCKSARGEN) 40% (World Bank, 2021)
 
The integrated project involves tracking complementary feeding practices and food patterns implemented in child development centers, day care centers, and other similar community facilities for children, and formulating interventions to ensure diversified food diversification.

The project also aims to produce a longitudinal study on the effects of intervention programs focusing on dietary diversification in addressing child malnutrition and stunting.

column4: Innovative Facility for Agricultural Sustainability: The Establishment of a State-of-the-Art Plant Disease Clinic Project with FFE
column6:
The emergence of plant diseases poses threats to agriculture, necessitating the establishment of a 
state-of-the-art plant disease clinic. As agricultural practices evolve, so must our approaches to diagnosing 
and managing these diseases. This request for infrastructure investment seeks to provide farmers, 
researchers, and agricultural professionals with the resources they need to effectively combat plant health 
issues. Equipped with advanced diagnostic technologies, a modern plant disease clinic would enable rapid 
identification of pathogens, ensuring timely intervention and mitigating crop losses. Moreover, this facility 
would serve as a hub for research and education, fostering collaboration between experts and practitioners. 
By integrating molecular techniques, the clinic could not only enhance diagnostic accuracy but also contribute 
to the development of novel disease management strategies. 
Investing in a state-of-the-art plant disease clinic is not merely about improving individual farm 
productivity, but a crucial step towards safeguarding food security. By equipping stakeholders with knowledge 
necessary to address plant diseases effectively, we can foster resilience in the agricultural systems and 
support sustainable food production. Therefore, the importance of this investment cannot be overstated, as it 
represents a commitment to advancing agricultural innovation, ensuring the health of our ecosystems, and 
promoting long-term sustainability and food security.

column4: Powering Growth in Banana Production and Value in Mindanao  through Innovative Formulation of Green Banana Saba-based  Healthy, Glutein-Free Pasta
column6:
The proposal aims to investigate the utilization of green banana flour, specifically derived from the Saba variety, as a key ingredient in pasta formulations. This initiative is rooted in several compelling reasons. 
The Philippines holds a significant position in the global banana market, ranking as the 3rd major exporter and the 5th major producer of bananas worldwide (PSA, 2023). Banana cultivation plays a crucial role in the nation's economy, supporting the livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers. By exploring the potential of Saba bananas as the 2nd highly produced banana in the country covering a land area planted of more than 200 has (PSA, 2023) for pasta development we can add value to this crop, thereby enhancing market opportunities and mitigating potential losses for farmers. 
Green bananas, particularly in the form of flour, offer notable nutritional benefits. They are rich in resistant starch and dietary fiber, which have been associated with improved gastrointestinal health and better glucose metabolism. 
Incorporating green banana flour into pasta formulations could enhance the nutritional profile of pasta, providing consumers with a healthier alternative, especially for those with dietary restrictions such as gluten intolerance. 

Furthermore, there is a growing demand for alternative and gluten-free food products globally. It is projected that Global Banana Flour Market Size will grow from USD 789.19 Million in 2022 to USD 1558.94 Million by 2032 according to a research report published by Spherical Insights & Consulting at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 7.04%.  Developing pasta formulations using green 
banana flour aligns with this trend, offering consumers a novel and nutritious option. The versatility of pasta as a widely consumed staple food presents ample market opportunities, both domestically and internationally.  
Lastly, the proposal underscores the importance of research and development in optimizing gluten-free pasta formulations. By leveraging innovative ingredients such as green banana flour, researchers can address the technological challenges associated with gluten-free pasta production and improve overall product quality, texture, and consumer acceptance In summary, exploring the potential of green banana flour in pasta development not only adds value to the abundant Saba banana crop but also addresses consumer demand for healthier and gluten-free food options. This initiative has 
the potential to contribute to the sustainability and growth of the agricultural and food sectors in the Philippines while meeting the evolving needs of consumers worldwide.

column4: Product Development and Commercialization of Indigenous Crop and Fish Products (MINSUPALA IRDC Project Phase 3)
column6:
The Product Development and Commercialization of Indigenous Crop and Fish Products (MINSUPALA IRDC Project Phase 3) is a 12-month collaborative R&D initiative led by the MINSUPALA Innovative Research and Development Consortium (IRDC), composed of 15 State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) across Central Mindanao. With a total funding of ₱117 million from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), the project aims to transform indigenous crops and fish species—identified and characterized during Phase 2—into innovative, market-ready products that promote food security, cultural preservation, and sustainable livelihood development.

Central Mindanao hosts a rich biodiversity of indigenous crops and fish species that hold deep cultural and economic significance for local communities. Building on previous assessments of water bodies, biodiversity, and socio-economic conditions, Phase 3 focuses on developing value-added products through improved processing, preservation, and packaging technologies. This includes pilot innovations such as drying, fermenting, pickling, powdering, and other traditional-and-modern hybrid techniques supported by scientific testing, sensory evaluation, and shelf-life analysis.

The project also strengthens community capacities by providing hands-on training for MSMEs, farmer and fisherfolk cooperatives, and SUC partners in food safety, good manufacturing practices, product development, branding, entrepreneurship, and market readiness. To ensure product viability, it will conduct market validation studies, develop prototypes, and facilitate market access through trade fairs, business-matching activities, and collaboration with agencies such as DTI, DA, DOST, and FDA/LGUs.

Ultimately, Phase 3 aims to bridge indigenous knowledge systems with modern food markets by developing shelf-stable and culturally rooted food products that enhance household incomes, diversify local food options, and promote regional identity. The initiative is expected to generate innovative indigenous products, establish market linkages, empower local enterprises, and strengthen the agri-fishery value chain, contributing significantly to regional socio-economic development and long-term food security.

column4: Production of Halâl-Compliant Raw Materials (soybean and corn) for Poultry Feeds
column6:
One of the latest projects implemented by the Southern Philippines Development Authority (SPDA) is the Poultry (Broiler Chicken) Production project. It is located in Barangay Labon, Sulop, Davao del Sur. The maximum capacity of the said poultry farm is 160,000 heads per cycle and it can operate at least 7 cycles per year. It is approximately 50 kilometers from the integrator’s dressing plant located in Sta. Cruz, Davao del Sur, and this project is in partnership with the San Miguel Foods Corporation.

The said project was created primarily to help augment the production of broiler chicken as the industry was extremely affected by the onslaught of the COVID-19 pandemic. The supply and demand gap is still evident up to the present time as manifested by a higher retail price of chicken compared to the pre-pandemic times. The continuously rising demand for chicken meat can be attributed to the rising population of Muslims not only in Mindanao but in the whole country in general. Based on the year 2020 Census of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), a total of 6,981,710 was recorded as a Muslim population . It is more or less 6.4% of the total population of the Philippines. As of 2022, it climbed to 7.9 million , or an increase of 11.6% in two (2) years.

Aside from the Muslim population, other religious groups like the Seventh Day Adventists (SDA) are also non-pork eaters which can be counted as an additional market for chicken not to mention those who have dietary requirements. Hence, offering halal food options in restaurants and hotels can attract more Muslim tourists and would enhance the country’s appeal as a tourist destination which is a boost to the tourism industry.

With the promising market for halal particularly chicken, the Authority envisioned becoming a major player in the industry because we believe that embracing halal practices in the Philippines serves both religious and economic purposes, promoting cultural diversity, economic growth, and international trade opportunities.

However, one of the long-standing challenges that the country has been encountering is the very limited supply of locally produced soybeans and corn which are considered as the major ingredients in the production of animal feeds. 

Correspondingly, the Philippines is currently the 41st largest importer of soybeans globally. Nearly 99% of the country’s soybean requirements are imported from the United States. In the year 2021 alone, the Philippines imported a total of $96.2 million worth of soybeans to sustain its requirements for food, animal feeds and other industries. The local production of soybeans, representing 1% of the total requirements which is approximately 2,000 to 3,000 tons per year is entirely used by the food industry.

Undoubtedly, the country relies on corn and soybean imports to sustain the requirements of its agricultural sector like the production of animal feeds and other industries.

In view of the foregoing premise, the Authority deemed it imperative to establish a sustainable source of Halâl compliant raw materials like corn and soybeans primarily to support not only the Authority’s requirements of the proposed Halâl Feeds project but also the requirements of the existing feed millers.
